trecho.0: the image glimmers, confronting both incompleteness and the blind saturation of visibilities and the tyranny of discourses. We stumble on the vertigo of the word, on the blindness of images. Not by chance, both questions important to Wagner Barja. Experiência Tumulto III, divided into two sessions, “Antologia” and the previously unseen installation “Jonas”, gathers his production made over three decades and which has always moved through diverse media and artistic expressions, through distinct domains, crossing and interrogating bodies of knowledge and sensibilities. We are introduced into a universe that overflows into “animaverbovocovisual” poems (his “obranomes”), installations and interventions, performances or videos. A profusion of images, objects and words, texts and characters that interweave, as if they founded or stirred up a world in continuous process of transmutation. A fabulous cosmogony in which bizarre creatures wander, strange hybrids, improbable encounters. Antologia is here the powerful visual-sonic-tactile notation of the world. Barja creates unexpected relations between the word, the image, the things and the beings, among the visual, sonic, tactile forms that cross his transit through the worl
trecho.2: over the contemporary gaze. Visions that, in the 1990s, incorporated opacity and the reworking of the very concept of seeing through the metaphor of blindness. In her suggestive itinerary, Panitz interweaves the hidden ribbons that link some works to others, points to the tenuous and revealing threads of light that are reflected and echo among them, to conclude that the results of Barja’s equations/works are angles that poeticize the world; in a playful and complex way they reconfigure it. Roland Campos, in his “Instantâneos da poesia visual brasileira”, reads AKD-MICO, which he considers a perfect rebus-poem, an installation that ferociously criticizes the artistic establishment by placing, behind a glass, bananas forming the letters AKD and, beside them, a marmoset that devours and disorganizes them, deforming the established model. And Barja laughs at the very unease he creates, placing behind another glass a second marmoset, itself eating the banana-letters POLE, carnivalizing the polemic itself by creating this obranome that affiliates Barja “to the lineage of visual poetry in which the charge of meanings is supplied by a collusion of the verbal with the non-verbal. In this case, with additions of irony”.
trecho.3: of Bataille, what is placed here is the anus through the body, through the eye, giving the latter an excretory function (by selection or digestion of what is seen). The concreteness (and the ephemerality) of the letters: The idea of “eating” ideas has belonged to us since, at the beginning of the 20th century, the native custom of anthropophagy was metaphorized, in the era of the discovery of the new world: we eat people, we eat cultures, we live the fantasy of the exit from barbarism (from animality) by swallowing what we wanted and what we did not want. Acknowledging the ascendancy both of the masters of 22 and of what Brazilian concrete poetry teaches, two objects/visual poems DO AKAD-MICO AO POLE-MICO play at undoing both the “law” of artistic production (and of thought) and its contestation. As promise and threat, the marmoset (in flesh, bone and figurative sense) aligns itself with the bananas that form the two prefixes, already asserting its ephemerality (its destiny is as clear as the gaze the marmoset casts upon them). The creature/box Cubo Cruz Lápide is eater and eaten at the same time, swallows the words like cube and vomits them with the cross. In this sense, Wagner describes this work as one of the first obranomes he built. Obranome always proposes, from its own enunciation, the passage from two-dimensionality to three-dimensionality and vice versa. In the case of the piece we are commenting on, it is the evolution from the cube to the cross; from the object inscribed in space to the plane, a passage that can obviously be carried out with other figures. For example, with the poemapolygon, in which one passes from the octagon to the polygon, which fully encompasses the whole concept of the exhibition “OBRANOME” (Brasília, Caixa, 2003). There, the term and the concept of obranome are defined as: “a Euclidean territory, octagonal in shape, static and two-dimensional. This octagon assumes another spatial premise and evolves to become a three-dimensional polygon, still in a static condition. Finally, in the third and fourth referentials, the space/time dimensions are configured. Thus, in a recent article on “A poesia que se vê”, Wagner Barja highlights the contribution of conceptual richness that Brazilian concrete poetry brought to artists linked to visual poetry. As, for example, the “Poemóbiles”, pieces of 1973 made by Augusto de Campos and the Spaniard Julio Plaza, where: “Verbo-visual language adopts three-dimensionality through interactivity. On leafing through the ”book-poem”, the message of a poetry of concrete root emerges, assisted by the movement that reaches space” (21). It is a matter of organizing the poem, independently of the verse, following graphic criteria that emphasize the materiality of the word and the spatiality of the page converted into an authentic sculptural support. A poem-object that “when the pages are opened, has its words projected forward, in various planes, suggesting multiple relations of meaning” (22). trecho.9: Among the works of Wagner Barja that can be classified as intersemiotic, I consider emblematic the “Acadêmico” A K D MICO (1986), published in the magazine Bric-à-brac IV. It is a perfect rebus-poem, in which the proposed verbal-visual charade, with the bananas moulding the letters A, K and D, and the figure of the marmoset capping the sequence, results in a biting message addressed to the artistic “establishment”. According to the Aurélio dictionary, a rebus is the “ideogram at the stage in which it ceases to signify directly the object it represents in order to indicate the phonogram corresponding to the name of that object”. And it is through this expedient that Wagner, with his satirical verve, sends a banana to the cultural immobilists on duty, urged to pay the monkey!
